I maintain that, for 2d image editing, 3d modeling and animation, sound design, spreadsheets, and similar productivity tools, the open source community has its head in the sand

WARNING: Rant incoming.

Many of the open source community that insists that the tools available for these professional tasks dabble in the areas of usage that these tools are used for, but next to none do these things as a living. They therefore refuse to accept that Gimp cannot serve as a replacement for photoshop for the professional artist, especially in industry, that Libre office sheets cannot reasonably be used by an accounting department in favor of excel, that blender does not serve large scale projects to nearly the same extent that autodesk maya does, or that audacity can't be used as a substitute for Avid Protools for those using protools to its greatest potential. After all, if THEY can use it, anyone can, even though the usecases of someone who occasionally uses blender to make something for their consumer 3d printer is FAR simpler to serve than the needs of a professional animator working on a major film (not to mention the value of support contracts and whatnot to corporate users). Gimp is suitable for someone who needs to edit their family photos, or do a bit of light editing to create an icon for a program they are writing, or even an independent artist that makes their keep doing small commissioned works, like logos or fanart or whathave you (though I do note that, of the dozen or so people I know personally who do such things for money, their first investment after a good graphics tablet is typically a license for photoshop, krita, inkscape, and gimp can only do so much. Intermediate users will push their limits, but will be generally satisfied, with perhaps a collection of minor annoyances. Advanced users will be actively hindered by these more basic tools), but is simply unacceptable for someone in professional content production (say doing textures for a triple A game). In addition to the lack of guaranteed support hindering corporate adoption, and even if we ASSUME an entire shop runs gimp despite this, and despite the fact that all good talent in the field will be more familiar with Photoshop, even if we ASSUME that that top grade talent is then trained with gimp to the point of being just as fluent with it as they are with photoshop, and ignore the collaboration issues from the lack of cloud features and whatnot, if we just look at the core, the act of producing content, these professionals WILL be able to do everything they were able to do in photoshop, BUT they will be slowed down by the tool they are using, either because of the need for workarounds to accomplish things that aren't fully functional, or due to a more barebones toolset.

I've noticed that the people who make these equivalence claims are usually the programmers (after all, the linux community is skewed pretty heavily towards developers). I am also a programmer, and understand the value of a good editor, regardless of which side of the IDE/Vim/Emacs holy war you might be on, so, to any programmer who makes these claims, would YOU say that windows notepad is a suitable replacement for your editor of choice? After all, notepad and a compiler can do all the same things that Emacs can, the workflow is just a bit different. Sure, a good programmer can still write their code in notepad, but at that point, the tool is significantly slowing you down, and while the alternatives available (say VisualStudio, or Clion) are far from perfect, they will be significantly less of a hindrance to you, at least if you would be making use of their advanced features (which yes, I know emacs and vim don't have. Their "advanced features" are their extensiblity). Artists are no different. Those of us who have had to work in closed source environments (despite recognizing and desiring the benefits of open) would REALLY be more open to change if you stopped being such prima dona's about your tools that are suitable for casual use, acceptable (if perhaps slightly lacking) for prosumer use, and downright deficient for professional users, if you stopped claiming those tools to be acceptable for those high level users. We haven't even touched on the benefits of increased adoption and training rate, of financially backed support, of features designed for group work. Hell, we see the same problems manifest in high end prosumer tools in these spaces for advanced users. Don't believe me? Look at adobe premier. It's not considered industry grade for television, marketing, or film, but it is VERY VERY close, and has quite a few more up and coming talent who are familiar with it than Avid, the industry standard non linear editor. It's not perfect. It's network rendering support pales in comparison to more powerful tools. Still, independent content houses use it for its price, and good integration with photoshop. Let's see what a high quality, efficiency minded professional video editor for one such small firm, who has had to use premier full time for years has to say about it. Yes. That's a thirty minute video with hundreds and hundreds of requests for simple features. He has several such videos, of similar length. He has a spreadsheet of close to 1000 bugs that cause him to change his workflow. Few of these feature requests and bugs have been addressed. Also remember that the rate at which adobe addresses such things is MUCH faster than the rate at which an open source project will. He is slowed down by this prosumer grade tool. And for the record, gimp is not where premiere is, Gimp is closer in quality to Sony Vegas. Good enough for basic work, and if you know it well, you can use it to approach the level of quality of the next tool up the totem pole, but not quite.

Rant over

If you need a tool for professional art, you aren't going to avoid photoshop unless you both work independently, and also value your time at less than the cost of such a tool. Similarly, while everything in a metal shop can be accomplished with a file, hand drill, blowtorch, and hammer, no one, not even a boutique knifemaker or sculptor who works alone, and doesn't need the capability for high volume, will turn down a good mill, grinder, lathe .etc.

If you are doing metalwork once a year, and getting the best possible results isn't a necessity, the file will do. If you just need to fix some red eye in a family photo, go right ahead, paint.net and gimp will suffice.
